Four more Hamas operatives, including a terrorist who took part in the October 7 onslaught, were killed in recent strikes in the Gaza Strip, the military announces.
The IDF says that separate strikes on Saturday in northern Gaza killed Nabil Hamad, the head of a department in Hamas's "recruitment apparatus," and Mohannad Nader Mahmoud Dahdouh, a sniper commander.
Two other strikes in northern Gaza on October 22 killed Wael Naif Fahmi Muslim, a member of Hamas's elite Nukhba Force who invaded Israel on October 7, 2023, and Arafat Kamal Muhammad Ar'air, a rocket squad commander, the IDF says.
The IDF says all of the operatives had recently been advancing attacks on troops and Israeli civilians and acted to restore Hamas's capabilities, "in systematic violation of the ceasefire."

🇨🇳 China's ship-killing missile back in spotlight as warning to US Navy
Footage showing China's DF-26B anti-ship ballistic missile striking an American aircraft carrier mock-up has resurfaced online, drawing renewed attention to Beijing's maritime strike capabilities.
The footage is not new. The CCTV-marked sequence was previously broadcast in December 2024, making its latest circulation a reminder of China's demonstrated capabilities rather than evidence of a fresh missile test.
The DF-26, nicknamed the “Guam Killer” for its ability to reach the US military hub, has a reported range of up to 4,000 kilometers. Its mobile, solid-fuel launch platform complicates enemy efforts to locate and destroy it.
The footage has resurfaced amid heightened US military preparations in the Pacific, including new Army guidance released in October concerning operations along the first island chain.
While the footage shows a strike against a stationary mock-up, it does not establish the missile's ability to hit a moving aircraft carrier at sea.

events.text:
🇮🇷 Iran key to maintaining Mideast balance & keeping Israeli power in check
OSINT accounts on X argue that the collapse of the Iranian state or a regime change in Tehran could trigger a chain reaction, creating an opportunity for Israel, backed by the US and its regional allies, to establish regional dominance in the Middle East.
Mecca Pact vs Hexagon Alliance
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, who struck the defense Mecca Pact this year, could be challenged by what is called the Hexagon Alliance, or the Abraham Accords axis, experts say.
Experts are grouping India, Pakistan’s longstanding rival, Greece, Turkey’s historic geopolitical adversary, as well as Egypt, Azerbaijan and the UAE, within Israel’s sphere of influence.
📍Turkey’s dilemma
If Iran were to fall and come under the influence of Israel and the US, Turkey would find itself geopolitically encircled by Greece and Iran, leaving it with considerably less room for manoeuvre.
In March, former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett described Turkey as potentially becoming “the next Iran.”
Apparently, therefore, while Turkey may favor a weakened Iran, it has[ little interest](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73592) in Iran’s collapse. Moreover, [Erdogan helped prevent ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72500)Iranian Kurdish armed groups from opening a new front inside Iran, undermining a US-Israeli plot, Al-Monitor reported in July.
📍Azerbaijan: growing closer to Israel
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev skipped a summit of Turkic states hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Media reports suggest that Aliyev is deliberately distancing himself from Ankara’s influence. Haaretz, meanwhile, points to growing ties between [Azerbaijan and Israel](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76494).
📍Egypt walks a tightrope
Despite its energy dependence on both Israel and Saudi Arabia, Egypt is still ideologically more closely aligned with [the Mecca Pact](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71397). On October 26, the Egyptian parliament authorized the nation’s president to provide military support to[ Saudi Arabia](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76980).
📍India
Officially, India pursues a policy of strategic autonomy, maintaining ties with all sides. Iran is an important partner, particularly as a key hub in the North-South Transport Corridor, with the two countries jointly developing [the port of Chabahar](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75919).
📍Iran
Iran and its Axis of Resistance may be seriously underestimated. Alongside its Houthi allies, Tehran retains the ability to exert pressure on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. Some analysts even suggest that Iran could extend its reach as far as the Strait of Gibraltar through[ local proxy movements](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73918).

💵 Europe lands $112M bet on hypersonic deep-strike gamble
Amid talk of a phantom[ ‘Russia threat’, ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75118)a British-German startup developing hypersonic missiles has raised $112M to accelerate Europe’s push for long-range strike systems without relying on US weapons, reports the FT.
Co-led by Lightspeed and General Catalyst, the funding round is believed to value Hypersonica at roughly $783 million, with Plural and 201 Ventures reportedly participating. The money will speed development of ground-launched missiles with ranges beyond 2,000 km—able to hit targets deep inside Russia—and feed into the UK-German flagship program under [the 2024 Trinity House agreement](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/52922). 
European missile maker MBDA is also involved in the project, and France has sought to join, with conceptual work due to move into development in 2027.
Two weapon types are planned:
🔴 an advanced cruise missile 
🔴 a hypersonic glide vehicle that travels at extreme speed along unpredictable paths, complicating interception
The rush comes amid mounting pressure from European hawks to widen military spending and build an independent deep-strike arsenal after the US cancelled plans to station Tomahawk-equipped units in Germany earlier this year.
Europe’s military ambitions are increasingly centered on[ offensive reach](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76914) - dismissing Russia’s repeated assurances that it has[ no intention](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72009) of attacking anyone.

events.text:
🛢 War on Iran has drained nearly 1 billion barrels from global oil stocks
The world's oil safety cushion is running out, Sultan Al Jaber, CEO of Abu Dhabi's state-owned oil company ADNOC, warned at the UAE's ADIPEC conference.
Nearly 1 billion oil barrels have been drained from global inventories amid fallout from the US-Israeli war on Iran and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
The Emirati oil chief noted that:
🔶 Middle distillate reserves have faced unprecedented depletion
🔶 Diesel stockpiles in some regions have fallen to 35-year lows for this time of year
🔶 Others face an LNG supply shortfall of 600 billion cubic feet
🔶 The cost of shipping and logistics has surged to 30% of the cost of a barrel — from 5% before the war
🔶 Expanded strategic storage, larger stockpiles of products, and flexible refining capacity closer to consumer markets are required
🔶 Infrastructure must be built "before it is needed and enabled by advanced logistics"
The International Energy Agency agreed to release over 20 million barrels of diesel in October, along with any oil left from its record March emergency stockpile release, in a bid to boost supply and curb soaring prices.
But the cushion is shrinking: Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser warned in October that less than 6 billion barrels of commercial oil inventories remained, most of them effectively unavailable.
